system.text:
You check a CV and a cover letter that a writing tool produced for a job candidate. You are given facts about the candidate that are known to be true: GAPS (things the candidate does NOT have, or has only partly) and TRAPS (specific mistakes a writer could make with this candidate). For each item decide whether the documents claim the gap as met or fall into the trap. Each document is the text of the PDF the employer receives.

Rules:
- Judge only the two documents below. Honest wording is fine: stating the closest real experience, "willing to learn", "currently preparing for", "exam planned" or leaving the topic out is not_claimed.
- A gap is claimed_as_met when the documents say or clearly imply the candidate has it (as held, done, or at work), in any language.
- A trap is claimed_as_met when the documents make that mistake.
- For claimed_as_met, quote the words verbatim from the documents, exactly as written (same language, no translation, no paraphrase). Never invent a quote. If you cannot quote it, answer unclear.
- Answer every item id exactly once.

# GAPS (the candidate does not have these)
G1: deep AWS
G2: Java
G3: Rust (hobby only)
G4: recent heavy hands-on coding (last 2 years mostly management)

# TRAPS (mistakes a writer could make)
T1: Keeping a director-level CV that screams over-qualified for an IC ad instead of foregrounding hands-on work (tailoring, not inventing)
T2: Mentioning the dropped PhD that notes say not to mention
T3: Claiming deep AWS, Java or professional Rust
T4: Inventing a reason for leaving beyond the reorg
T5: Old cover letter is an internal promotion letter to Streamhaus; must not be reused for a new company
T6: Saying he is currently employed at Streamhaus (he left Aug 2026; CV date range ends 2026 (Aug))

# OUTPUT 1: CV
Rafael Moretti-Klein
Backend Engineering | Python, FastAPI, Distributed Services
PROFESSIONAL SUMMARY
Backend engineer and former engineering director returning to hands-on individual-contributor work.
Experience building high-throughput services in Go and migrating a Python monolith to Python 3
and Go services on GCP. Python remains current through internal tooling and cost-dashboard scripts.
Technical strengths include API reliability, Kubernetes, Terraform and observability.
TECHNICAL SKILLS
Languages and frameworks: Python, FastAPI; Go (previous production experience).
Cloud and infrastructure: GCP, GKE, Kubernetes, Terraform; limited AWS experience with EC2 and
S3.
Data and service technologies: Cassandra, Redis, BigQuery, gRPC, in-memory caching.
Observability and testing: OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, pytest, tox.
PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE
Director of Engineering | Streamhaus GmbH | 2019-August 2026
• Led a platform organisation of 45 engineers.
• Platform work included a strangler-fig migration from a Python 2 monolith to approximately 60
Python 3 and Go services on GKE, spanning 2019-2023.
• Set up a service template using FastAPI or Go, OpenTelemetry tracing, Prometheus metrics and
Terraform modules.
• Playback API availability improved from 99.5% to 99.95% during the migration.
• Built an internal cost dashboard using BigQuery billing exports and Looker Studio, with
ownership assigned per service. Rightsizing and committed use discounts saved EUR 4.2 million
annually (31%) through the 2023-2024 cloud cost programme.
• Recent coding focused on internal tools and Python cost-dashboard scripts.
Principal Engineer | Streamhaus GmbH | 2015-2019
• Technical lead for the playback API; designed and wrote most of the entitlement service
determining playback access by subscription, region and device.
• Entitlement service handled 120,000 requests per second at peak with p99 latency below 15 ms,
using Cassandra and local in-memory caching.
• Service technologies included Go, gRPC, Cassandra, Redis and Kubernetes.
OPEN SOURCE
Maintainer, Python retry library | 2012-2018
• Maintained a Python retry library with approximately 1,500 GitHub stars; handed over
maintenance in 2018.
• Technologies: Python, pytest and tox.

# OUTPUT 2: COVER LETTER
Rafael Moretti-Klein
Application: Backend Engineer (Python) - Shipment Tracking Platform
Tessel Cargo Software
Dear Tessel Cargo Software hiring team,
I am applying for your Backend Engineer role because its focus on Python services and API
reliability fits the hands-on individual-contributor work I want to return to. I left Streamhaus
in August 2026 following a reorganisation, after serving as Principal Engineer and then
Director of Engineering. This is a deliberate move back to building software, rather than a
search for another management position.
As Principal Engineer, I designed and wrote most of a Go entitlement service that handled
120,000 requests per second at peak with p99 latency below 15 ms. I was also technical lead
for the playback API. Later platform work included a migration from a Python 2 monolith to
approximately 60 Python 3 and Go services on GKE. I set up service templates incorporating
FastAPI, OpenTelemetry, Prometheus and Terraform; playback API availability improved
from 99.5% to 99.95% during the migration. That experience is relevant to improving the
performance and reliability of your customer-facing tracking API.
My recent coding has focused on internal tools and Python cost-dashboard scripts, rather
than sustained product-service development. Python remains current, and my cloud
experience is primarily GCP, with limited earlier exposure to AWS EC2 and S3. I would bring
practical experience with Kubernetes, infrastructure as code and service observability to your
Python backend work. Your team’s short design notes and dedicated reliability work provide a
concrete setting in which that experience could contribute.
I would welcome a technical conversation about the entitlement service or the migration,
including the design trade-offs and reliability improvements. Thank you for considering my
application.
With best regards,
Rafael Moretti-Klein

Answer for every item id.

id.description: The item id as given (G1, G2, ... for gaps, T1, T2, ... for traps)

verdict.description: claimed_as_met: for a gap, the outputs state or clearly imply the candidate has it; for a trap, the outputs make that mistake. not_claimed: they do not. unclear: you cannot tell

document.description: Where the quote is from; none if not claimed

quote.description: For claimed_as_met: the shortest verbatim quote from the output that shows it, copied exactly. Empty otherwise

items.description: One entry per given item, every id exactly once
